title: Reliability update: regional failover automation + Dedicated protections
summary: Redwood shared an update on the Reliability Program work focused on regional failover automation (signal hierarchy, guardrails/rollback, observability) and how Dedicated customers are protected during regional impairment and during planned controlled failover tests (“game days”). Atlas asked about blast radius, change approvals, data residency constraints, audit evidence, and how/when Redwood communicates during planned tests vs real incidents. Redwood confirmed Dedicated traffic is isolated, failover automation is gated (per-tenant limits + optional approval hooks), and planned tests will have explicit opt-in/notice plus tight scopes. Next steps include sharing the comms playbook, audit event schema/retention guidance, and aligning a customer-specific “do not fail over across residency boundary” policy.
topics: Why failover automation is being upgraded (noisy triggers, slow detection, hard validation)
Trigger signal hierarchy and corroboration (reachability, 5xx burn, tail latency burn, capacity)
Anti-flap and rollback semantics (hold-down timers, rate limits, auditability)
Dedicated protections: pool drain/evacuation sequencing and capacity headroom checks
Planned controlled failover tests: scope, success criteria, rollback conditions, customer notifications
Audit logs and evidence requests for enterprise compliance
Data residency boundaries and cross-region routing constraints
next_steps: Redwood to send Atlas the regional failover communication playbook + status page template language.
Redwood to share a short write-up of Dedicated-specific safeguards (drain gates, per-tenant flip limits, approval hooks).
Atlas to confirm residency boundaries (allowed regions) for both prod and DR, and whether cross-region is permitted for any traffic classes.
Schedule a 30-min technical follow-up with Atlas SRE to review failover policy config and “no-failover” scenarios.
action_items: Lauren Bishop (Redwood) - Email planned game day notification draft + how we’ll scope Dedicated tenants (by 2026-01-26).
Rafael Mendes (Redwood) - Share current go/no-go criteria checklist and what telemetry we watch during a regional event (by 2026-01-29).
Miles Thornton (Redwood) - Provide audit event schema fields + retention defaults and how customers can request export (by 2026-01-29).
Samantha Reed (Atlas) - Confirm data residency/failover boundaries and any contractual constraints for cross-region processing (by 2026-02-02).
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-01-22
Start time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Title: Reliability update: regional failover automation + Dedicated protections

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Lauren Bishop, Rafael Mendes, Miles Thornton, Dev Patel
Atlas Payments: Samantha Reed, Jon Wu, Priya Desai

---

[00:00] Lauren Bishop: Hey everyone. Thanks for making time. This one is basically a reliability update, focused on the regional failover automation work we’ve been doing, and specifically how it applies to Dedicated customers like you all.

[00:13] Samantha Reed: Sounds good.

[00:14] Jon Wu: Yep, we’ve got a few questions from the last… I guess the planned routing test thing.

[00:20] Lauren Bishop: Totally. And Priya, good to see you as well.

[00:22] Priya Desai: Hi, thanks.

[00:25] Lauren Bishop: Quick agenda: we’ll cover what’s changing, what’s not changing, how planned tests work, how we communicate, and then open Q&A. Rafael and Miles are here for the guts of the system. Dev can speak to comms and support escalations.

[00:43] Rafael Mendes: Hey.

[00:44] Miles Thornton: Hi all.

[00:46] Dev Patel: Hello.

[00:48] Lauren Bishop: Alright. So high level: today failover is… a mix. Some routing is automated but the triggers can be noisy and the rollback behavior wasn’t deterministic enough. That creates risk: false positives, or slow detection when a region is actually impaired.

[01:08] Lauren Bishop: The project is to tighten the trigger signal pipeline, add guardrails and deterministic evaluation, and validate it end to end through controlled failover tests. That includes Hosted API and Dedicated capacity.

[01:22] Samantha Reed: When you say “controlled tests,” you mean in production?

[01:26] Lauren Bishop: Some are in staging first, then limited production with explicit success criteria and rollback conditions. We’ll get into how we keep blast radius small.

[01:35] Jon Wu: Ok.

[01:36] Lauren Bishop: Miles, do you want to explain the trigger hierarchy piece in plain English?

[01:42] Miles Thornton: Yeah. The biggest change is we’re standardizing what signals can cause the system to say “this region is unhealthy” and then “we should shift traffic.”

[01:54] Miles Thornton: The hierarchy is basically: reachability and network-level symptoms are most authoritative, then 5xx error burn, then tail latency burn, and capacity exhaustion is sort of a gating factor and also a “don’t overload the other region” factor.

[02:12] Priya Desai: Reachability meaning like, can you even get to the region from outside?

[02:15] Miles Thornton: Exactly. Synthetic probes plus internal signals. Think: canaries from multiple vantage points, plus control plane connectivity. If we can’t reach the region, we don’t wait for application-level 500s to pile up.

[02:29] Jon Wu: And what about partial issues? Like, one model pool is degraded but the region isn’t dead.

[02:35] Miles Thornton: That’s one of the reasons we’re adding corroboration and scoping. The automation doesn’t just flip everything immediately. It evaluates per route / per service slice. Also we have hold-down timers so it doesn’t flap.

[02:49] Rafael Mendes: And to be clear, for Dedicated, we’re not treating you like general shared traffic. Your routing policy is separate and we can enforce per-tenant safety limits.

[03:00] Samantha Reed: Ok. The thing we care about is, we don’t want a “helpful” failover to cause overload in the target region and then we’re down in both.

[03:10] Rafael Mendes: Yep. That’s a top design constraint. The automation uses capacity headroom as a gate. If the target region doesn’t have headroom, it won’t push the full shift. It can do partial shedding and return a controlled overload response rather than melt down.

[03:27] Jon Wu: What does “controlled overload response” mean? Like 429?

[03:31] Rafael Mendes: It can be 429 or a 503 with Retry-After semantics depending on the route. The goal is clients back off. We’re also tuning gateway retry budgets to avoid a thundering herd.

[03:45] Lauren Bishop: And we can share client retry guidance too. Some of that came out of the January test.

[03:51] Samantha Reed: Yeah, we saw some streaming disconnects in that window.

[03:55] Miles Thornton: That was a known issue. The redirect + streaming reconnect path was not as robust as it should be. There’s a fix in flight that improves idempotency and reconnection behavior when a stream is moved across regions.

[04:09] Jon Wu: Ok. On triggers: you said noisy. What was noisy?

[04:14] Miles Thornton: In staging we saw tail latency spikes that were localized to one upstream dependency and not a region impairment. If you used only p99 latency as the trigger, you’d fail over too aggressively.

[04:28] Miles Thornton: So now it’s “latency burn” using a burn-rate window plus it needs corroboration—either errors, reachability, or a specific dependency health signal. Also dampening: a minimum duration above threshold.

[04:44] Priya Desai: Is there an audit trail for these decisions? That’s one of our requirements.

[04:49] Miles Thornton: Yes. Every recommendation and every execution and rollback emits an audit event: who/what/why, the signal evidence, timestamps, and the policy diff.

[05:01] Priya Desai: Who is “who” if it’s automated?

[05:04] Miles Thornton: The actor is recorded as the controller service identity, plus the on-call acknowledgement if approvals are required. If it’s fully automated for a scope, it still records the controller as actor and links to the evaluated evidence.

[05:20] Samantha Reed: Approvals required… is that always on for Dedicated?

[05:24] Rafael Mendes: Right now, for production, yes for most Dedicated scopes we’re keeping an approval hook. Basically dry-run computes the action, posts a summary, and the on-call can approve. Over time, for well-behaved tenants and well-tested paths, we can talk about removing it.

[05:44] Jon Wu: So there’s a “dry-run” mode in prod?

[05:46] Rafael Mendes: Exactly. It evaluates the same signals and produces “recommended policy flips” but doesn’t execute. That’s how we validate without risking customer impact.

[06:02] Lauren Bishop: And for planned tests, we can pre-announce that we’re going to run dry-run first, then execute a limited flip for a subset of traffic.

[06:11] Samantha Reed: Ok, say more about blast radius. What’s “subset” mean? Specific models or…

[06:17] Rafael Mendes: Multiple ways. It can be per tenant, per route, per model group, or even a small percentage-based canary if your integration can support it.

[06:29] Miles Thornton: For Dedicated, we also coordinate with pool drain automation. Before shifting, we can drain a portion of the GPU pool in the source region to reduce new admissions and let in-flight requests complete, depending on the scenario.

[06:44] Jon Wu: That drain automation is new, right?

[06:46] Miles Thornton: It is being formalized. Previously it was pretty manual and runbook-driven. Now it’s a controlled workflow with progress metrics.

[06:57] Samantha Reed: What does “drain” actually do? Stops new requests?

[07:00] Miles Thornton: Stops placing new work, gradually reduces concurrency, and then evacuates pods/workers depending on the pool. For Dedicated it’s careful: it won’t kill active long streams without coordination—there are timeouts and sequencing.

[07:16] Priya Desai: From a compliance standpoint, we also need to understand data residency. We can’t just “fail over” across the Atlantic.

[07:24] Lauren Bishop: Totally. Let’s talk about that explicitly. For your Dedicated deployment, we can set hard boundaries: allowed regions for failover. If a region is not allowed, the controller will not route there, even if it’s healthy.

[07:39] Priya Desai: Is that policy enforced at the routing layer?

[07:42] Rafael Mendes: At the policy evaluation layer, yes. It’s deterministic. It’s not “best effort.” And the audit event will show “blocked by residency policy” if it would otherwise have failed over.

[07:55] Jon Wu: Ok, but then what happens if the allowed region is down and there’s no second allowed region?

[08:00] Rafael Mendes: Then we degrade in place: controlled overload responses, possibly shedding, and we page humans. Basically we don’t violate residency. That’s the tradeoff.

[08:11] Samantha Reed: Makes sense.

[08:13] Lauren Bishop: For Atlas specifically, we should confirm what your DR assumption is. You’ve talked about EU-only processing. Is there a second EU region you consider acceptable?

[08:23] Samantha Reed: We’re evaluating eu-west and… we call it eu-central. We’re not live in the second region yet, but we want that path.

[08:31] Lauren Bishop: Got it. That’s a good follow-up: we’ll align on allowed region set and we can plan tests once the second region is ready.

[08:41] Priya Desai: And we need audit log retention. What’s your default?

[08:46] Miles Thornton: For failover audit events, we’re targeting at least 90 days default retention in the platform logs, longer for enterprise tiers. We can export on request. I’ll send specifics—don’t quote me on exact number if your contract has something else, but that’s the direction.

[09:04] Dev Patel: Support can also attach those audit summaries to an incident ticket if you open one, so you have a single thread.

[09:13] Jon Wu: Communication: during a planned test, are you going to post on the public status page?

[09:18] Dev Patel: We have a playbook. For planned tests that might have any customer-visible blip, we typically post a “maintenance / reliability test” notice with wording that it’s controlled and limited scope. For truly no-impact dry-run, we don’t.

[09:36] Dev Patel: For Dedicated, we also do direct comms: email to your on-call distro and, if we have Slack Connect, we can post there. And during the window, we’ll give updates at a set cadence.

[09:50] Samantha Reed: Ok, we prefer direct comms. Public status pages are fine but we don’t want to discover it from Twitter.

[09:56] Lauren Bishop: Yep. For Dedicated accounts we treat it as “proactive notify.”

[10:01] Priya Desai: Who approves the messaging? Internally.

[10:04] Dev Patel: On-call incident commander approves real incident updates. For planned tests, it’s usually SRE lead + the account owner. For high sensitivity, leadership sign-off.

[10:16] Jon Wu: Can you share the template? Like the exact phrasing.

[10:19] Dev Patel: Yes, we can share the template language and the cadence expectations.

[10:27] Samantha Reed: Can we go back to “false positives”? What’s preventing a false positive from flipping us during a normal jitter event?

[10:34] Miles Thornton: Three layers: (1) signal corroboration and hierarchy, (2) dampening timers and minimum time unhealthy, (3) rate limits and anti-flap—max flips per tenant per hour, plus hold-down after a flip.

[10:51] Miles Thornton: Also there’s a concept of “confidence” in the decision—basically evidence count. In dry-run we output that so humans can judge.

[11:01] Jon Wu: Confidence score makes me nervous. Is it a model?

[11:04] Miles Thornton: No, not ML. It’s more like a deterministic rubric: which signals fired, how many probes, burn-rate windows, and so on.

[11:13] Jon Wu: Ok.

[11:15] Rafael Mendes: And for Dedicated, we can also set “do not fail over” for certain routes. For example if you have a route that absolutely cannot move, we can prevent it.

[11:25] Samantha Reed: That’s important. Our payments authorization path is more sensitive than, say, internal analytics.

[11:30] Lauren Bishop: Makes sense. That’s a configuration conversation.

[11:36] Priya Desai: During failover, is any customer data replicated cross region? Like prompt logs or traces.

[11:42] Rafael Mendes: For Dedicated, by default we don’t replicate payload logs cross region without explicit configuration. Metrics are aggregated, but raw payload is controlled by your logging settings.

[11:54] Priya Desai: Aggregated metrics can still be sensitive depending on labels.

[11:58] Rafael Mendes: Yep, and we’ve been reviewing metric cardinality and labels. We avoid tenant identifiers in shared metrics. For your Dedicated environment, we can keep metrics within your allowed region set as well, depending on setup.

[12:12] Samantha Reed: Ok. What did you learn from the January game day? Not the marketing version, like the real issues.

[12:19] Miles Thornton: Fair. Real issues: one, we saw latency spikes in the target region due to client retry behavior and a too-aggressive gateway retry budget. Two, dashboards lacked annotations, making it harder to correlate. Three, a hold-down timer triggered a rollback earlier than expected.

[12:41] Jon Wu: So it rolled back even though the source region was still “bad”?

[12:44] Miles Thornton: Source region was partially recovered; the system interpreted it as enough to revert, but we decided the threshold was too eager. That’s being tuned.

[12:55] Rafael Mendes: Also we had a staging crash earlier during rehearsal when a signal stream was missing. We fixed that with a null handling path and added a regression test.

[13:08] Samantha Reed: Good.

[13:10] Lauren Bishop: And we want to run these tests quarterly, but only once we’re confident the guardrails are solid.

[13:17] Jon Wu: Quarterly in prod? For everyone?

[13:20] Rafael Mendes: Not for everyone at once. Think: a small subset, rotating. The idea is to keep muscle memory and validate that the system still works as dependencies evolve.

[13:32] Samantha Reed: I like the idea but we need opt-in or at least notification.

[13:36] Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated, yes: proactive notification and you can opt out for a period if you have a peak event.

[13:44] Priya Desai: And for regulated periods like end-of-quarter, we may need a blackout window.

[13:49] Lauren Bishop: We can accommodate blackout windows.

[13:53] Jon Wu: Can you describe the actual failover mechanism? Is it DNS? Anycast? Or app routing?

[13:59] Miles Thornton: It’s mostly application-layer routing policies plus some DNS TTL tuning. We don’t rely solely on DNS because TTL caching can be unpredictable.

[14:10] Jon Wu: Ok, because we’ve been burned by DNS TTL not respecting.

[14:13] Miles Thornton: Yeah, exactly. We treat DNS as one lever, but primary is policy-based routing at the gateway / routing layer. It can shift quickly and we can roll back with guardrails.

[14:28] Samantha Reed: During a failover, what does a client see? Redirect? Or same endpoint?

[14:32] Rafael Mendes: Typically same endpoint. Internally we route you to a different region. In some cases for streaming we might return a redirect-like response, but we’re moving toward transparent routing where possible.

[14:46] Jon Wu: If it is a redirect, our client has to handle it. We can, but we want to know.

[14:51] Rafael Mendes: Understood. We’ll document the behavior per endpoint and recommended retry patterns.

[15:01] Lauren Bishop: And we can run a quick client readiness check with your team.

[15:06] Samantha Reed: Cool.

[15:07] Priya Desai: On SLOs: do you have a “multi-region availability SLO” that applies to Dedicated?

[15:13] Rafael Mendes: We do. It’s measured as availability of the service across the allowed regions, but it’s nuanced: a partial degradation in one region is not necessarily a “region-level event.”

[15:26] Priya Desai: That nuance is always the hard part.

[15:29] Rafael Mendes: Yep. We define what constitutes a region-level impairment versus a local service issue. The new dashboards help on-call distinguish that.

[15:41] Jon Wu: Does the failover controller integrate with your incident tooling? Like timeline events.

[15:46] Miles Thornton: Yes. It emits timeline markers and incident-bot summaries. That also helps postmortems auto-populate milestones.

[15:56] Samantha Reed: That’s good.

[15:58] Lauren Bishop: Let’s talk about how Dedicated is protected specifically. Miles mentioned drain automation. Rafael mentioned per-tenant safety limits. Anything else?

[16:07] Rafael Mendes: Dedicated is isolated capacity, so the blast radius from shared traffic is already reduced. Second, we have per-tenant flip limits: max number of routing policy changes per time window. Third, the controller can be scoped by tier and tenant.

[16:24] Rafael Mendes: Fourth, before doing a failover, we validate cross-region reachability with synthetic probes. Fifth, capacity headroom checks in the target region, and if not enough, we prefer partial shedding instead of full shift.

[16:41] Jon Wu: Partial shedding meaning you’d reject requests rather than route?

[16:44] Rafael Mendes: Yes, with explicit Retry-After so clients can backoff.

[16:50] Samantha Reed: So basically you’d rather fail “cleanly” than succeed and overload.

[16:54] Rafael Mendes: Exactly.

[16:58] Priya Desai: How do you ensure that your controller doesn’t become a single point of failure?

[17:03] Miles Thornton: Good question. The controller is not in the request path. If it’s down, routing keeps the last known policy. The region health service has caching and TTL to avoid stampedes.

[17:18] Jon Wu: Ok.

[17:19] Lauren Bishop: Another big theme is observability. We’re adding dashboards for reachability, error burn, latency burn, capacity, and policy flips. And crucially: annotations when automation acts.

[17:32] Samantha Reed: Can we get access to those dashboards?

[17:35] Lauren Bishop: For your Dedicated environment, we can provide the relevant views or exports. Some internal panels are Redwood-only, but we can share what’s customer-facing.

[17:46] Jon Wu: At least give us the signal definitions, because we’ll ask “why did you fail over.”

[17:50] Miles Thornton: Yep. The audit event will include the evidence, but we’ll also share the definitions.

[18:00] Samantha Reed: Ok.

[18:02] Lauren Bishop: I want to check: are there any open incidents or lingering concerns from your side about the January planned test?

[18:10] Jon Wu: We saw a small spike of 5xx and some streaming resets. It wasn’t catastrophic but it got attention.

[18:18] Dev Patel: That aligns with what we saw. If you want, we can send the internal summary and the remediation items. The streaming fix is the key one.

[18:27] Samantha Reed: Please.

[18:28] Priya Desai: I’d like the audit log sample too.

[18:31] Miles Thornton: I can provide a redacted sample event.

[18:34] Priya Desai: Great.

[18:36] Lauren Bishop: Let’s do Q&A. Anything else on the planned tests?

[18:42] Samantha Reed: Are you planning another one soon?

[18:45] Rafael Mendes: Likely a smaller scope one in Q1/Q2, but we’re tightening blast radius. We’d notify you ahead of time and likely do dry-run first.

[18:56] Samantha Reed: Ok.

[18:58] Jon Wu: I have a technical question: during a failover, how do you avoid double spending capacity due to retries? We see clients retry aggressively.

[19:07] Rafael Mendes: Two things: gateway retry budgets are being tuned, and we’re standardizing Retry-After. Also we’re recommending idempotency keys for certain operations. For streaming, reconnection logic is updated so reconnect doesn’t start a totally new generation unless necessary.

[19:24] Jon Wu: Ok, so you’re pushing idempotency to the client for safety.

[19:28] Rafael Mendes: Where appropriate, yes.

[19:31] Priya Desai: For approval hooks: is there a path where we can require manual approval always for our tenant?

[19:38] Lauren Bishop: Yes, we can keep approvals on for your scope. It might increase failover time, but it meets control requirements.

[19:46] Priya Desai: We might do that initially.

[19:48] Samantha Reed: We can revisit when we trust it.

[19:52] Miles Thornton: Also worth noting: even with approvals, detection and recommendation can be fast, so human time is the main factor.

[20:01] Jon Wu: What are you targeting for detection-to-failover time, like in seconds?

[20:06] Rafael Mendes: For a true region impairment with reachability loss, we want detection under a minute and routing action shortly after, but it depends on hold-down and corroboration settings. We can share the target deltas.

[20:22] Samantha Reed: Under a minute is good.

[20:24] Lauren Bishop: Anything on capacity planning? We’ve talked about headroom.

[20:29] Samantha Reed: Yeah, do you reserve headroom for DR?

[20:33] Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated, we plan capacity with failover scenarios in mind. There’s a “safe to failover” criteria based on baseline load and drain rates. Vanessa’s team manages that, but the controller consumes the headroom signal.

[20:50] Jon Wu: If headroom is insufficient, do you alert us? Like “you’re not actually HA right now.”

[20:56] Lauren Bishop: That’s a good ask. We can provide a periodic report or alert when you’re below a failover-ready threshold.

[21:06] Samantha Reed: Please. That’s useful for internal reporting.

[21:10] Priya Desai: And it helps with risk documentation.

[21:12] Lauren Bishop: Got it.

[21:14] Jon Wu: Another question: you mentioned reachability probes. From where? If it’s only from your cloud, it might not reflect customer paths.

[21:22] Miles Thornton: Multiple vantage points. Some are within the provider, some external. We’re also integrating synthetic probes that simulate client traffic patterns across regions.

[21:35] Jon Wu: Ok.

[21:36] Samantha Reed: Any competitor note: we’re also looking at Bedrock for some workloads. They claim multi-region endpoints. How do you compare?

[21:44] Lauren Bishop: The big difference is control and auditability. We give you deterministic policies, per-tenant constraints, and clear audit trails. Also Dedicated isolation and performance tuning. But we can do a separate comparison call if helpful.

[21:58] Samantha Reed: Not necessary now.

[22:00] Priya Desai: On audit logs: do they include signal values? That could be considered operational data but not customer data.

[22:07] Miles Thornton: Yes, it includes which signals fired and their evaluated state, not raw payload. For example “reachability_probe_failed=3/3” or “5xx_burn_rate exceeded.”

[22:20] Priya Desai: Ok.

[22:22] Dev Patel: And if you ever need an attestation after an event, Support can provide an incident summary with those timestamps.

[22:31] Samantha Reed: Good.

[22:33] Lauren Bishop: Let’s make sure we capture the specific follow-ups: comms playbook and templates, Dedicated safeguards doc, audit event sample, and residency boundary config.

[22:44] Samantha Reed: For residency boundary: we’ll confirm our allowed region set. For now, do not fail over outside EU.

[22:52] Lauren Bishop: Understood.

[22:54] Jon Wu: One more: how do you prevent oscillation? Like region A bad, flip to B, then A looks good, flip back, then A bad again.

[23:03] Miles Thornton: Anti-flap is a combination of hold-down timers after a flip, plus “require sustained health” before revert, plus action rate limiting. Rollback is not immediate unless there’s evidence the failover itself caused harm.

[23:20] Jon Wu: That last part is important. If failover causes overload, you might want to partially roll back.

[23:25] Miles Thornton: Exactly. Rollback semantics include “revert” and also “hold” where we stop further shifts and shed.

[23:33] Samantha Reed: Ok.

[23:35] Priya Desai: Is there human override? Like can you force it to stay in one region.

[23:40] Rafael Mendes: Yes, on-call can freeze automation or force a policy state. It’s all audited.

[23:47] Priya Desai: Great.

[23:49] Lauren Bishop: Anything else before we wrap?

[23:52] Samantha Reed: Just reiterating: notifications matter. We want heads-up for tests, and for real incidents we want a direct line.

[23:59] Dev Patel: Totally. We’ll make sure your on-call distro and escalation path is current.

[24:05] Jon Wu: Also please send client retry guidance for streaming.

[24:08] Rafael Mendes: Will do.

[24:10] Lauren Bishop: Ok, we’ll send a recap email with links and owners. Thanks everyone.

[24:16] Samantha Reed: Thanks.

[24:17] Priya Desai: Thank you.

[24:18] Jon Wu: Thanks.

[24:20] Lauren Bishop: Bye.
